t: Say what they're doing, like a sports commentator: "You're pushing the car. Up the hill!"
While you dress them, say each step: "Arm in. Other arm. Head through. Peekaboo!"
Talk through what you're doing in the kitchen: "I'm stirring. Round and round. It's hot."
Be the narrator, not the director: describe their play instead of asking them to do something.
Look where they're looking, then name it: "A dog! A big, fluffy dog."
Add one word to theirs. If they say "car", you say "Red car." If they say "more", say "More milk, please."
Name a feeling you see: "You look cross. The tower fell down."
Use describing words at meals: crunchy, soft, warm, sour.
Use position words in passing: in, on, under, behind, next to.
Sing what you're doing to a tune you know: "This is the way we brush our teeth…"
Sing a song and stop before the last word. Wait for them to fill it in.
Hum the same short song at every nappy change or bath. Routines love a soundtrack.
Offer two choices: "Blue cup or green cup?" Hold both up and wait for a point.
Let them choose the bedtime book, even if it's the same one again.
Ask "Which way shall we go?" at the next corner, and go that way.
Ask a 'what' or 'where' question about a picture, then wait a full five seconds.
At the end of the day ask: "What made you laugh today?" and tell them yours.
Wonder out loud: "I wonder where that bird is going?" No answer needed.
Take turns, then wait. Count to five in your head before you speak again.
Put your phone in another room for the next ten minutes.
When they bring you something, stop, look at it, and say thank you.
Get down to their eye level for the next thing they show you.
Copy a sound or a movement they make, then see if they copy you back.
Notice when they're done. Say "All finished?" and move on together. Endings matter too.
Give a 'thank you' that names what they did: "Thank you for carrying the spoons."
